blocks.body:
A smooth complex surface defined by a polynomial equation, such as $x^4 + y^4 + z^4 + w^4 = 0$ in complex projective space, is at the same time three kinds of object: a topological space with holes of various dimensions, a manifold on which one can do calculus with complex coordinates, and an algebraic object built from polynomials. Each viewpoint produces its own invariants. The Hodge conjecture predicts exactly which topological features come from algebra: which "holes" can be filled or traced out by subvarieties cut out by polynomial equations.

This page builds the minimum vocabulary (projective varieties, cohomology, types $(p,q)$), states the conjecture, and explains the cases that are known.

blocks.title: The objects
blocks.body:
Complex projective space $\mathbb{CP}^n$ is the set of nonzero vectors $(z_0, \dots, z_n) \in \mathbb C^{n+1}$ up to scaling by nonzero [[complex-numbers|complex numbers]]. A projective variety $X \subset \mathbb{CP}^n$ is the common zero set of finitely many homogeneous [[polynomials-roots|polynomials]]; it is non-singular if at every point the gradients of the defining polynomials have the expected rank, so that $X$ is a complex manifold. A complex manifold of complex dimension $n$ has real dimension $2n$. A curve ($n = 1$) is a real surface; a non-singular plane cubic curve is topologically a torus.

Inside $X$ we can look for algebraic subvarieties $Z$: subsets of $X$ cut out by further polynomial equations. If $Z$ has complex codimension $p$ in $X$, it has real dimension $2n - 2p$.

blocks.title: Cohomology and the Hodge decomposition
blocks.body:
Cohomology measures holes. The group $H^k(X,\mathbb Q)$ is a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb Q$ whose dimension $b_k$ (the $k$-th Betti number) counts the independent $k$-dimensional holes. For a torus $b_0 = 1$, $b_1 = 2$, $b_2 = 1$. One concrete model: $H^k(X,\mathbb C)$ is the space of closed differential $k$-forms modulo exact ones (de Rham cohomology), and the rational classes $H^k(X,\mathbb Q)$ sit inside it as those whose integrals over all $k$-dimensional cycles with integer coefficients are rational.

In complex coordinates $z_j = x_j + iy_j$ every form is built from $dz_j = dx_j + i\,dy_j$ and $d\bar z_j = dx_j - i\,dy_j$. A form has type $(p,q)$ if each term contains $p$ factors $dz$ and $q$ factors $d\bar z$. Hodge's theorem says that on a non-singular projective variety this splitting passes to cohomology:

$$H^k(X,\mathbb C) = \bigoplus_{p+q=k}H^{p,q}(X), \qquad \overline{H^{p,q}} = H^{q,p}.$$

The Hodge numbers $h^{p,q} = \dim H^{p,q}$ satisfy $b_k = \sum_{p+q=k}h^{p,q}$ and $h^{p,q} = h^{q,p}$. For a curve of genus $g$: $h^{1,0} = h^{0,1} = g$ and $b_1 = 2g$.

blocks.title: Why subvarieties give (p,p) classes
blocks.body:
A subvariety $Z$ of codimension $p$ defines a class $[Z] \in H^{2p}(X,\mathbb Q)$: it is the class that, paired with a closed form $\eta$ of degree $2n-2p$, gives $\int_Z\eta$. Integrals over $Z$ of forms with integer periods are integers, so the class is rational.

It is also of type $(p,p)$. The reason is that $Z$ is itself complex, of complex dimension $m = n - p$. Restricted to $Z$, a form of degree $2m$ can only survive if it has type $(m,m)$: a term with more than $m$ factors $dz$ vanishes on an $m$-dimensional complex manifold, just as $dz_1\wedge dz_1 = 0$. So $\int_Z\eta$ only sees the $(m,m)$ part of $\eta$, and this forces $[Z]$ to lie in $H^{p,p}$. Rational linear combinations of such classes are called algebraic classes.

blocks.title: Hodge classes
blocks.body:
The Hodge classes of degree $2p$ on $X$ are the elements of

$$\operatorname{Hdg}^p(X) = H^{2p}(X,\mathbb Q)\cap H^{p,p}(X).$$

They are the cohomology classes that pass both tests satisfied by algebraic classes: they are rational, and they have type $(p,p)$.

blocks.title: The Hodge conjecture
blocks.body:
Let $X$ be a non-singular complex projective variety. Then every Hodge class is algebraic:

$$H^{2p}(X,\mathbb Q)\cap H^{p,p}(X) = \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q}\{[Z] : Z \subset X \text{ an algebraic subvariety of codimension } p\}.$$

The inclusion $\supseteq$ is the argument above; the conjecture is the inclusion $\subseteq$. Hodge raised the question in 1950.

blocks.title: What is known
blocks.body:
- Lefschetz $(1,1)$ theorem (Lefschetz, 1924; later reproved by Kodaira and Spencer): the conjecture holds for $p = 1$, and even with integer coefficients. Hodge classes in $H^2$ are classes of divisors.
- Using the hard Lefschetz theorem, the case $p = 1$ implies the case $p = n - 1$. Since $p = 0$ and $p = n$ are trivial, the conjecture holds for all varieties of dimension at most $3$. The first open case is $p = 2$ on fourfolds.
- The integral version is false: Atiyah and Hirzebruch (1962) found torsion integral classes that are not algebraic, and Kollár gave non-torsion examples. That is why the conjecture is stated over $\mathbb Q$.
- For general compact Kähler manifolds, which need not be projective, the natural analogue fails (Voisin, 2002).
- Evidence: Cattani, Deligne and Kaplan (1995) proved that the locus where a class stays Hodge, in a family of varieties, is algebraic, which the conjecture predicts. Deligne showed that Hodge classes on abelian varieties are "absolute Hodge", a weaker algebraicity property.

blocks.title: Holomorphic forms vanish on complex curves
blocks.body: In $\mathbb C^2$ with coordinates $(z, w)$, restrict the forms $dz\wedge dw$ (type $(2,0)$) and $dz\wedge d\bar z$ (type $(1,1)$) to the complex line $w = az + b$, parametrised by $z = s + it$ with real $s, t$.
blocks.solution:
On the line, $dw = a\,dz$, so $dz\wedge dw = a\,dz\wedge dz = 0$. In real terms the coefficient of $ds\wedge dt$ is $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial s}\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial t} - \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial t}\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial s} = 1\cdot ai - i\cdot a = 0$.

For $dz\wedge d\bar z$ the coefficient is $1\cdot(-i) - i\cdot 1 = -2i$, so $dz\wedge d\bar z = -2i\,ds\wedge dt$, a nonzero multiple of the area form. Integrals of $(2,0)$ forms over complex curves are always $0$; only the $(1,1)$ part of a $2$-form can be detected by a complex curve. This is the mechanism that puts algebraic classes in $H^{p,p}$.

blocks.title: Curves: the conjecture is easy
blocks.body: A non-singular plane curve of degree $d$ has genus $g = (d-1)(d-2)/2$. Compute $g$ for $d = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ and explain why the Hodge conjecture is trivially true for curves.
blocks.solution:
The genera are $0, 0, 1, 3, 6$. So lines and conics are spheres, cubics are tori, and quartics have three handles.

For a curve ($n = 1$) the only possible $p$ are $0$ and $1$. $H^0$ is spanned by the class of the whole curve, and $H^2(X,\mathbb Q)$ is one-dimensional, spanned by the class of a point (a codimension $1$ subvariety). Both are algebraic, so every Hodge class is algebraic. The interesting middle group $H^1$ has odd degree and contains no Hodge classes at all.

blocks.title: Hodge numbers of surfaces in projective 3-space
blocks.body: For a non-singular surface of degree $d$ in $\mathbb{CP}^3$ one has $b_1 = 0$, Euler characteristic $\chi = d^3 - 4d^2 + 6d$, and $h^{2,0} = \binom{d-1}{3}$. Compute $b_2$, $h^{2,0}$ and $h^{1,1}$ for $d = 4$ and $d = 5$, and check $d = 1, 2$ against known spaces.
blocks.solution:
Since $b_0 = b_4 = 1$ and $b_1 = b_3 = 0$, $b_2 = \chi - 2 = d^3 - 4d^2 + 6d - 2$, and $h^{1,1} = b_2 - 2h^{2,0}$.

- $d = 1$: $\chi = 3$, the Euler characteristic of the projective plane. $d = 2$: $\chi = 4$, that of $\mathbb{CP}^1\times\mathbb{CP}^1$, which is what a smooth quadric is.
- $d = 4$ (a K3 surface): $b_2 = 22$, $h^{2,0} = 1$, $h^{1,1} = 20$.
- $d = 5$: $b_2 = 53$, $h^{2,0} = 4$, $h^{1,1} = 45$.

For a quartic surface, which classes in the $22$-dimensional $H^2(X,\mathbb Q)$ are Hodge depends delicately on the coefficients of the equation: the rational classes lying in the $20$-dimensional subspace $H^{1,1}$ form a space whose dimension (the Picard number) depends on the equation and always lies between $1$ and $20$. Lefschetz's theorem guarantees that all of them are classes of curves on the surface. The conjecture asks for the same phenomenon in higher codimension, where no analogue of Lefschetz's proof is known.

blocks.body:
- Both conditions matter. Classes of type $(p,p)$ with complex coefficients are far more numerous; the conjecture concerns rational classes of type $(p,p)$.
- The integral Hodge conjecture is false; use $\mathbb Q$.
- Non-singular and projective are essential hypotheses; the analogue for general compact Kähler manifolds fails.
- Known low-dimensional cases come from $p = 1$; they do not suggest a method for $p = 2$.

The conjecture lives where [[complex-numbers|complex analysis]] ([[holomorphic]]) meets the algebra of [[polynomials-roots|polynomial equations]] and topology. Its arithmetic cousins, the Tate conjecture and the conjectures on algebraic cycles, connect with [[bsd]] and with the zeta functions of varieties over [[finite-fields]]. It is one of the Millennium problems with [[rh]], [[p-vs-np]], [[navier-stokes]], [[yang-mills]], [[bsd]] and the solved [[poincare]].

1. Show that a form of type $(2,0)$ on $\mathbb C^2$ restricts to zero on every complex line.
2. Verify $b_2 = 22$ for the quartic surface from the Euler characteristic formula, and explain why $h^{2,0} = h^{0,2}$.
3. Why can odd-degree cohomology contain no Hodge classes?
4. Compute $h^{1,1}$ for a non-singular surface of degree $6$ in $\mathbb{CP}^3$.

Voisin, Hodge Theory and Complex Algebraic Geometry I
Griffiths & Harris, Principles of Algebraic Geometry

blocks.body:
Imagine living inside a finite universe with no edge. How could you tell whether it is shaped like a three-dimensional sphere or like something more complicated? One test: tie a loop of string through space, starting and ending at you, and try to reel it in without cutting it. On a sphere every loop can be reeled in. Poincaré asked in 1904 whether this single test is enough to recognise the $3$-sphere.

The answer is yes. Grigori Perelman proved it in 2002–03, using Richard Hamilton's Ricci flow, an equation that smooths the geometry of a space the way heat smooths temperature. It is the only Millennium Prize Problem solved so far. This page explains the statement, the two-dimensional analogue, the idea of Ricci flow, and the history.

blocks.title: Manifolds and loops
blocks.body:
An $n$-dimensional manifold is a space that looks, near each point, like ordinary $n$-dimensional space $\mathbb R^n$. A closed manifold is one that is compact (finite in extent) and has no boundary. Examples in dimension $2$: the sphere, the torus (surface of a doughnut), the surface of a pretzel with $g$ holes. The $3$-sphere $S^3$ is the set of points at distance $1$ from the origin in $\mathbb R^4$, a closed $3$-manifold.

Two spaces are homeomorphic if there is a continuous bijection between them with continuous inverse: they are the same up to stretching and bending, without tearing or gluing.

A space is simply connected if every closed loop in it can be continuously shrunk to a point while staying in the space. The sphere $S^2$ is simply connected. The torus is not: a loop going once around the hole cannot be shrunk.

blocks.title: The Poincaré conjecture (Perelman's theorem)
blocks.body: Every closed, simply connected $3$-manifold is homeomorphic to the $3$-sphere $S^3$.

blocks.title: The two-dimensional picture
blocks.body:
For surfaces the analogous statement has been known since the nineteenth century, as part of the classification of closed surfaces. Every closed orientable surface is a sphere with $g \ge 0$ handles, and $g$ is determined by the Euler characteristic $\chi = V - E + F$ of any subdivision into polygons: $\chi = 2 - 2g$. Only the sphere ($g = 0$) is simply connected, because each handle carries a loop that cannot be shrunk.

Geometry gives another view. The Gauss–Bonnet theorem says that the total curvature of a closed surface is $\int K\,dA = 2\pi\chi$. Every closed surface carries a metric of constant curvature (the uniformisation theorem), and Gauss–Bonnet fixes its sign: positive for the sphere, zero for the torus, negative for $g \ge 2$. In dimension $2$ topology is controlled by a "best" geometry. Thurston's geometrisation conjecture (1982) proposed a similar but more intricate picture in dimension $3$: every closed $3$-manifold can be cut along spheres and tori into pieces, each carrying one of eight model geometries. The Poincaré conjecture is a special case.

blocks.title: Why dimension three was the hard case
blocks.body:
The natural generalisation, that a closed $n$-manifold with the same homotopy type as $S^n$ is homeomorphic to $S^n$, was proved first in high dimensions. Smale proved it for $n \ge 5$ in 1961 (other proofs were given by Stallings and Zeeman): in high dimensions there is room to move obstructions out of the way. Freedman proved the case $n = 4$ in 1982, by very different methods. That left $n = 3$, where neither technique works.

Poincaré had first conjectured that having the same homology as the sphere would suffice. In 1904 he constructed a counterexample to that stronger claim: the Poincaré homology sphere, which has the homology of $S^3$ but whose loops cannot all be shrunk; its fundamental group (the group of loops) is the binary icosahedral group, of order $120$. This is why the conjecture is stated with simple connectivity.

blocks.title: Ricci flow
blocks.body:
A Riemannian metric $g$ on a manifold tells you lengths and angles, and hence curvature. The Ricci curvature $\operatorname{Ric}(g)$ is a kind of average of sectional curvatures in each direction. Hamilton (1982) introduced the Ricci flow,

$$\partial_t g = -2\operatorname{Ric}(g),$$

which evolves the metric in time. It behaves like a heat equation for the metric: regions of positive curvature contract, regions of negative curvature expand, and irregularities tend to spread out. Hamilton proved in 1982 that a closed $3$-manifold with a metric of positive Ricci curvature flows, after rescaling, to a metric of constant positive curvature, so it is a quotient of $S^3$.

For general metrics the flow develops singularities: thin necks pinch off, for example. Perelman's work (three preprints of 2002–03) controlled the singularities with new monotone quantities (an entropy functional and a "no local collapsing" theorem), classified what the geometry looks like near a singularity, and showed how to perform surgery: cut out a neck, cap the two ends with balls and restart the flow. For a simply connected manifold the flow with surgery becomes extinct in finite time, and running the surgeries backwards shows the manifold was a sphere. The same method proves the full geometrisation conjecture. Detailed expositions by Kleiner and Lott, by Morgan and Tian, and by Cao and Zhu checked the argument in the following years.

blocks.title: The shrinking round sphere
blocks.body: The round sphere $S^n$ of radius $r$ has metric $g = r^2 g_1$, where $g_1$ is the unit sphere metric, and $\operatorname{Ric}(g) = (n-1)g_1$, independent of $r$. Solve the Ricci flow starting from radius $r_0$ and find when it becomes extinct.
blocks.solution:
Look for a solution $g(t) = r(t)^2g_1$. Then $\partial_t g = \frac{d}{dt}(r^2)\,g_1$, and the equation becomes

$$\frac{d}{dt}(r^2) = -2(n-1), \qquad\text{so}\qquad r(t)^2 = r_0^2 - 2(n-1)t.$$

The sphere shrinks and disappears at $T = \dfrac{r_0^2}{2(n-1)}$; for $S^3$ that is $T = r_0^2/4$. Its shape stays perfectly round the whole time. Finite-time extinction of this kind is exactly what Perelman proved happens, after surgeries, for every simply connected closed $3$-manifold.

blocks.title: Euler characteristics
blocks.body: Compute $V - E + F$ for the surface of a cube, an octahedron, and a torus made from an $n \times m$ grid of squares with opposite edges glued. Check Gauss–Bonnet for a round sphere of radius $r$.
blocks.solution:
Cube: $8 - 12 + 6 = 2$. Octahedron: $6 - 12 + 8 = 2$. Both are spheres, $g = 0$.

Torus grid: after gluing there are $nm$ vertices (one per grid point, with the edges identified), $2nm$ edges (one horizontal and one vertical starting at each vertex) and $nm$ squares, so $\chi = nm - 2nm + nm = 0$, giving $g = 1$.

Round sphere: curvature $K = 1/r^2$ everywhere and area $4\pi r^2$, so $\int K\,dA = 4\pi = 2\pi\cdot 2$. The radius cancels, as it must for a topological invariant.

blocks.title: A group of order 120
blocks.body: The binary icosahedral group can be realised as a set of unit quaternions. Generate the group from $a = \tfrac12(1 + i + j + k)$ and $b = \tfrac12(\varphi + \varphi^{-1}i + j)$, where $\varphi = (1+\sqrt5)/2$, and count its elements.
blocks.solution:
First, both are unit quaternions: $|a|^2 = \tfrac14(1+1+1+1) = 1$, and $|b|^2 = \tfrac14(\varphi^2 + \varphi^{-2} + 1) = \tfrac14(3 + 1) = 1$ using $\varphi^2 + \varphi^{-2} = 3$.

Multiplying them together repeatedly (a computer does this in a moment) produces exactly $120$ distinct unit quaternions, closed under multiplication. This finite group is the fundamental group of the Poincaré homology sphere, which is the quotient $S^3/\Gamma$ of the unit quaternions $S^3$ by this group $\Gamma$. So that space has a loop that cannot be shrunk, even though its homology agrees with that of $S^3$.

blocks.body:
- Simply connected is about loops, not about holes in the sense of homology; the Poincaré homology sphere shows the difference.
- The theorem is about closed manifolds. $\mathbb R^3$ is simply connected but not compact, and is not a sphere.
- Ricci flow alone does not prove the theorem; singularities form, and the surgery and its control are the heart of Perelman's work.
- In dimension $4$ the smooth version (is every smooth homotopy $4$-sphere diffeomorphic to the standard one?) is still open; Freedman's theorem is topological.

The proof combines geometry, analysis of partial differential equations (Ricci flow is a nonlinear heat equation, compare [[navier-stokes]] and [[fourier-poisson]]) and topology. Perelman declined both the Fields Medal (2006) and the Millennium Prize (2010). The other Millennium problems are [[rh]], [[p-vs-np]], [[navier-stokes]], [[yang-mills]], [[hodge]] and [[bsd]]; gauge theory from [[yang-mills]] is also a central tool in four-dimensional topology.

1. Compute $V - E + F$ for a tetrahedron and for a dodecahedron.

3. For the round $S^2$ of radius $r_0$ under Ricci flow, find the extinction time.
4. Show that the product of two unit quaternions is a unit quaternion, so that $S^3$ is a group.

Morgan & Tian, Ricci Flow and the Poincaré Conjecture
